Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 17, 1920 Patrick Parizeau Box 277 Monroe, Washington My Friend: I am sending you herewith check No. 1613 in the sum of $5.00 payable to the order of Patrick Parizeau, which I hope you will make good use of. Very truly yours, Special Agent in Charge. :MG Enc. Washington State Reformatory Monroe, Wash. April 10, 1920 Dear Sir, Will I wish I was in Cushman now, if you would let me go home when I asked you I would not be here. I wish you would send my Indian progress here and also I have money left their I wish you would send it here and will you please get my suit and thing from Antoine Parisian and send it here too. Where is Ted and Alex at? I heard they are back in school. Sure is a beautiful day. to be out. I wasn't so bad before I got in here but I might be a d—good fellow when I go out. I'll be my own boss then. I wish you would look it over. Good by. Your Friend Patrick A. Parisian address to—Mr C W Peel. Sept. Cushman Agency Tacoma Wash 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Flathead Agency, Dixon, Montana, January 8, 1920. Mr. C. V. Peel, Special Agent in Charge, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Sir: Referring to your letter of the 5th inclosing letter written by Gus White, step father of Patrick Parizeau, I have to advise that there appears no necessity for Patrick to return to his home to assist his step father, and all such requests should be disregarded and Patrick should remain at his studies. The step-father is not overly-inclined to work and this is just an excuse to have Patrick return home in order that he may do the work and Gus White, the step-father, secure most or all of the results of the labor of Patrick. Respectfully, [signature] Superintendent. Barium Mountain Dec 14 19— Dear Steppe Sam, I will drop you a few lines to let you know I am well and hoping you are the same. Well, Pat—I would like to have you home to help me to cut some wood try to come home before Christmas. We are having lots of snow here. How is the weather over to Lemishmen? Tell Dushie we find Bob. She is fat and happy they are fat and Spencer he is fat too. Bernie is often poor since I came back from hunting. Well I will close my last letter hoping you will come soon. Tell Christine I send my best love and wishes and love to from your Stanley Steppe father. Good By Eyes White Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 14, 1920 Patrick Pariseau c/o Disciplinarian Cushman Indian School Dear Patrick: I am just in receipt of a letter from Mr. Sharp, your Superintendent, advising that it is not necessary for you to return to your home to assist your step-father, and that you should remain at this school and continue your studies. You should, therefore, remain here and continue your studies and work, and make every effort to improve your mind and knowledge of work before you become a man. I shall make an effort to watch your progress and see that you get every benefit that the school can give. So I will expect you to knuckle down to hard study and work and think no more of returning home until the end of the school year. Your friend, Special Agent in Charge. CVP:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 5, 1920 Theodore Sharp, Supt. Flathead Indian Agency Dixon, Montana My dear Sir: I am enclosing herewith a letter just received by Patrick Pariseau from his step-father requesting him to come home and help cut some wood. Please look into the matter and advise me whether you think it advisable for Pat to come home. I am advised that he has been persistent in his requests to be permitted to go home, but that Mr. Hammond has always refused to grant his requests. It is rather a hard matter for us to keep the children contented when their parents are continually writing them to come home. Awaiting your early reply, I am Very truly yours, Special Agent in Charge. CVP:MG Enc. Roman, Montana Dec. 17, 1919 Dear Step Son: I will drop you a few lines to let you no I am well and hoping you are the same. Well, Pat, I would like to have you home to help me to cut some wood. Try to come home before Christman. We are having lots of snow. How is the weather over to Cushman. Is there lost of Snow. Tell Duchie we finde Bosie. She is fat and the horses they are fat and Spencer he is fat too, but Bennie is afle poor. Since I came back from hunting. Well I will close my sorte letter hoping you will com soon. Tell Antoine I send my best love and wishes, and Louie, too, from your truly Step-father. Goodbye. CUS WHITE #370. Sir: You will find enclosed herewith postal card received from Patrick A. Parizeau in which he makes a request for $25 and states that he is not attending school at the present time. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 19, 1919 Dear Mr. Fisk: You will please begin on the bathing outfit in Girls' home No. 2, and complete the repairs without delay. Then take up the bathing equipment in Boys' Home No. 2. These two jobs will take precedence over all others. Very respectfully, E. H. HAMMOND Superintendent. BHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 18, 1919 Mr. Theodore Sharp, Supt. Flathead Indian Agency Dixon, Montana Dear Mr. Sharp: I received your letter regarding Pat Pariseau's request for money and have noted particularly his statement that "he was not in school, etc." none of which is true. Pat has been in school regularly since his arrival, October 26th. About the time he wrote the letter to you, he and the Disciplinarian had a difference in opinion as to the need of swearing at the waitresses in the dining room and the Disciplinarian got the best of the argument. Pat has been inclined to pose as a buckaroo, but he met his match in the Disciplinarian, who called his bluff. I have not heard anything as to Pat's misconduct since. If Pat has any money available, I recommend that he pay at least part of his tuition. It would perhaps make him appreciate the opportunities offered him, if he realizes is paying for them. Wishing you a very Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year, I am Very sincerely, Superintendent. EHH:MC Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 26, 1919 Theodore Sharp, Supt. Dear Sir: There is enclosed herewith check No. 11910 in the sum of $25.00, drawn on the account of Patrick Parizeau, and I request that this amount be placed to his credit. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington. April 23, 1917. Mr. Fred C. Morgan, Supt., Flathead Indian Agency. Dear Sir: Pat Paricau and Clarence Michell left Cushman School without permission on April 17, two days after the close of the school. The last we heard of them they were at Ellensburg on their way home. As I had no funds to send for them, and owing to the fact that school had closed, I have taken no steps to secure their return. Very respectfully, Superintendent. Ronan Mont. October 10, 1919. Dear Sir, My Boy Pat went to school when he was six years old. It taught to be enough school for him. He's nineteen years old now. And I'm going to keep him home. I'd like to see where you got right to use his money. You every read the Law how it reads? I don't believe you got got right to use his money. I seen the letter you wrote to his mother. I got two more boys this I never signs for them to stay two or three years. The has boy paid their own fare and there own expense is the government never spent a cent for them to go. I don't see where you got rights to hold Pat's money. Send his money right away. I'm going to keep him home to work here. Your respectfully, Mr. Gus White Ronan Mont Box #3710 Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Oct. 15, 1919 Mr. Gus White Ronan, Montana Dear Sir: I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of October 10, 1919. This has been sent to the Superintendent, Mr. Sharp, for his information. Unless there are other reasons than your desire to keep Pat home to work, he will have to return to school, or will have to pay all the expenses incurred in bringing him back to School. Very truly yours, Superintendent. This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every instance. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. If the name of parent or guardian is dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. Applicable laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. 5-297 h FARMING.
